original_question: Can one identify abstract classes of variational objectives on probability measures and corresponding random approximations such that the objective values E(mu_n) converge to E(mu_*) as the number of samples grows, quantitative convergence rates can be proved under explicit model assumptions, and the resulting abstract classes still cover problems of practical interest in machine learning?
target_in_paper: Section II-C, labeled "Open Problems"—specifically the first, theoretical open problem stated immediately after the setup of a population objective on measures and its random approximation in Section II-B (eqs. (3)–(4)). This paper does not contain a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3; the nearest official formulation is this Section II-C question. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual theoretical question. It correctly asks for abstract classes of objectives on probability measures together with random approximations, asks for objective-value convergence of the form E(mu_n) to E(mu_*), asks for quantitative rates under explicit assumptions, and insists that the abstract framework should still cover machine-learning problems of practical interest. That is essentially the content of the theoretical open problem in Section II-C. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))
missing_details: The paper first sets up the population/approximation framework: one has a population objective E on an admissible class of probability measures over some space, and in practice only an approximate random objective E_n is optimized. Your draft should state that optimization setup explicitly, not just the limit statement. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))

The roles of mu_* and mu_n should be spelled out: mu_* is the optimizer (or target optimal measure) for the population objective E, while mu_n is the optimizer produced from the approximate/random objective E_n. The draft currently mentions only their objective values. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))

The paper is broader than a pure sample-size asymptotic: E_n may arise from finite samples, modeling limitations, or optimization/surrogate constraints. So 'as the number of samples grows' is slightly narrower than the paper’s wording; the paper’s variable n indexes a refinement of the approximation more generally. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))

The target of classification is a class of pairs (E, E_n), not one single objective. The draft should make clear that the problem is to identify abstract families for which the convergence/rate theory works. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))

The paper’s 'practical interest' is clarified by Section IV: the intended coverage includes generative modeling, uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution generalization, and weak-information disambiguation. Naming this scope makes the question more stand-alone and paper-faithful. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))

No algebraic data such as ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or a clause like 'for all sufficiently large m' belongs here; those notions are not part of this paper’s setup and should not be imported. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))
refined_question: Let M be a class of probability measures on a space Z, let E:M→R∪{+∞} be a population variational objective with optimal measure mu_* in argmin_{mu in M} E(mu), and let E_n be a random approximate objective on M—arising, as in the paper, from finite data, modeling limitations, or surrogate/optimization constraints—with optimizer mu_n in argmin_{mu in M} E_n(mu). Can one identify abstract classes of such pairs (E, E_n) for which E(mu_n) converges to E(mu_*) as n→∞, obtain quantitative convergence rates under explicit model assumptions, and show that these classes still cover machine-learning problems of the kind highlighted in the paper (such as generative modeling, uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution generalization, and weak-information disambiguation)? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))
justification: The draft is targeting the first question in Section II-C, not the second, more practical question that follows it. Section II-B introduces exactly the population objective on measures and its approximate random surrogate; Section II-C then asks for abstract classes of objectives/approximations yielding convergence and rates; Section III sketches the intended proof avenues (classical empirical-process bounds, Hilbertian metrics, sigma-fields, epi-convergence); and Section IV explains what 'practical interest' means through four concrete application families. Because this is a vision/open-problem paper, there is no sharper numbered theorem/conjecture nearby to replace the Section II-C formulation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/2306.11928))
